layer: South Carolina / Horry County regulatory layer — artificial turf installation
applies_to: The South Carolina (Horry County) portion of the service-area polygon: Myrtle Beach, North Myrtle Beach, Surfside Beach, Conway, Loris, Little River, Longs, Wampee, Adrian, Allen, Hand, Carolina Forest, Socastee, Aynor, Briarcliffe Acres, plus unincorporated Horry County. Murrells Inlet is Georgetown County and was NOT researched in this layer. The Brunswick County, NC portion (Shallotte, Carolina Shores, Sunset Beach, Ash, Pireway, Longwood, Reeves, Holden Beach) is a separate legal regime and is NOT covered here.

findings.fact: Horry County's stormwater utility ordinance expressly enumerates BOTH layers of an artificial turf system as impervious. Sec. 17.7-16 (and identical language at Sec. 17.7-1): "Impervious surfaces are those areas which prevent or impede the infiltration of stormwater into the soil as it entered in natural conditions prior to development. Common impervious surfaces include, but are not limited to, rooftops, sidewalks, walkways, patio areas, driveways, parking lots, storage areas, compacted gravel and soil surfaces, awnings and other fabric or plastic coverings, and other surfaces which prevent or impede the natural infiltration of stormwater runoff which existed prior to development." Artificial turf is not named — but a turf system is a plastic covering laid over a compacted gravel base, and both of those phrases appear verbatim in the list.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the single most consequential regulatory fact in the county. It is ordinance text, not inference: the two components of every turf install he does are individually named as impervious. On any commercial job in unincorporated Horry County this can push the parcel into a higher stormwater fee tier, and on a large job it changes the post-development runoff calculation. He needs a documented answer for this on every commercial bid — and he should get a written determination from Horry County Stormwater rather than assume. Note the definition is a performance test ("prevent or impede the infiltration ... as it entered in natural conditions"), so a genuinely free-draining system with infiltration data is arguable — but the burden is on him.
findings.confidence: high — retrieved verbatim from the Municode-published Horry County Code, code current through Aug 12 2026

findings.fact: North Myrtle Beach has an explicit, recently enacted performance pathway that lets a surface be excluded from impervious calculations. Sec. 23-129.4 (added by Ord. No. 25-45, adopted 10-6-2025) — "Standards for pervious surfaces and impervious surfaces for single-family and duplex residences not subject to site-specific development plan review": to be considered pervious a material or system must (a) be installed so water infiltrates through the surface into the ground; (b) "Demonstrate a minimum infiltration rate of two (2) inches per hour, based on manufacturer testing or accepted industry standards"; (c) be installed to manufacturer spec including required base materials; (d) pass inspection; (e) be maintained. It closes with: "If these criteria are not met, the surface will be considered impervious, regardless of material type or labeling." It adds: "This standard applies regardless of native soil conditions. Site-specific soil testing is not required." The matching NMB zoning definition reads: "Impervious surface: A surface that prevents or significantly impedes the infiltration of stormwater into the ground. This includes but is not limited to roofs, buildings, concrete, asphalt, pool decks, patios, compacted gravel, and pavers not meeting the definition of a pervious surface. Surfaces shall be considered impervious unless demonstrated otherwise in accordance with the performance criteria set forth in section 23-129.4."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the most actionable single fact for the business. In North Myrtle Beach artificial turf CAN be counted pervious — but only if he can hand the building department manufacturer test data showing the installed system (turf + pad + base) achieves 2 inches/hour, and only for single-family and duplex jobs not going through site plan review. It also means the default is against him: "surfaces shall be considered impervious unless demonstrated otherwise." Getting a 2 in/hr certified spec sheet from his turf supplier and a standard base detail is a concrete, do-it-this-week task that unlocks NMB residential work and is a genuine differentiator over competitors who show up without paperwork. Note also "compacted gravel" is named impervious by default here too.
findings.confidence: high — retrieved verbatim from the Municode-published North Myrtle Beach Code, code current through Jul 23 2026

findings.fact: Myrtle Beach's ZONING code defines impervious more broadly than its stormwater chapter, and its enumerated list captures the turf base course. Zoning Appendix A, Sec. 203: "Impervious Surface: Any material that prevents, impedes, or slows infiltration or absorption of storm and surface water directly into the ground at the rate of absorption of vegetations-bearing soils." And: "Impervious Surface Coverage: The percentage of net land area of the lot covered by impervious surface. For the purpose of computing impervious lot coverage, the following items and like installations are considered impervious: building coverage, parking lots, parking structures, driveways, side-walks, patios, pool decks, wooden decks, grouted cut stone or tile walkways, and stone, shell or gravel surfacing." Separately, Myrtle Beach's stormwater chapter (Sec. 18-3) uses a narrower, older definition: "Impervious surface means a surface that has been compacted or covered with a layer of material so that it is highly resistant to infiltration by water. The term includes most conventionally surfaced streets, roofs, sidewalks, parking lots and other similar structures."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Two different tests inside one city. The zoning benchmark is the rate of absorption of vegetation-bearing soils — i.e. compared against live lawn, which is exactly what turf replaces, so turf loses that comparison unless he can show otherwise. And "stone, shell or gravel surfacing" is expressly impervious, which is the aggregate base under every install. On a Myrtle Beach commercial job the zoning impervious-coverage cap is likely the binding constraint, not the stormwater chapter. He should quote and price against the zoning definition, not the stormwater one.
findings.confidence: high — retrieved verbatim from the Municode-published Myrtle Beach Code, code current through Feb 16 2026

findings.fact: Horry County's stormwater utility fee is calculated directly from a parcel's impervious percentage. Sec. 17.7-17: non-single-family properties get a "development intensity factor" from a published table — 90–100% impervious = 0.95; 75–89.9% = 0.80; 55–74.9% = 0.65; 30–54.9% = 0.40; 10–29.9% = 0.20; 1–9.9% = 0.05; less than 1% = 0.01 — billed per 20,000 sq ft of land area, with a minimum threshold charge of $0.75/month ($9.00/year) on all properties. Sec. 17.7-18 provides a credit against the service charge for developed land (other than detached single-family) with on-site detention or retention facilities that "reduce or mitigate the impact of impervious surfaces on the subject property," per the county's stormwater utility service charge credit manual.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Gives him a dollar-denominated conversation with commercial clients: if turf is counted impervious it can move a parcel up a tier and raise the annual stormwater bill. Conversely, the on-site retention credit is a sales angle worth chasing — a turf system built over a deep stone drainage reservoir may be creditable, but that has to be confirmed against the county's credit manual before he ever puts it in a proposal. Do not claim the credit until the county confirms it in writing.
findings.confidence: high — ordinance text; the credit's applicability to turf is explicitly NOT established

findings.fact: Myrtle Beach and North Myrtle Beach both bill stormwater on an impervious-area unit. Myrtle Beach Sec. 18-3: "Equivalent residential unit (ERU) means the average impervious area of a representative sample of all developed residential properties in the single family residential category. The equivalent residential unit is 5,000 square feet of impervious surface area." North Myrtle Beach Sec. 15-92(c): "The stormwater utility fee shall be based on an 'equivalent runoff unit' (ERU) defined as three thousand five hundred (3,500) square feet of impervious area, which is the average impervious area for a single-family home in the city."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Quantifies the downside if turf is classed impervious: a 2,000 sq ft backyard turf install is roughly 0.4 of a Myrtle Beach ERU or 0.57 of a North Myrtle Beach ERU. That is a small number for a homeowner and a real number on a commercial site — useful for framing honestly rather than being ambushed by it at permit time.

findings.fact: Horry County requires a stormwater permit at half an acre of land disturbance. Horry County Stormwater Management Design Manual (January 2024), Sec. 2.3: "All land disturbance activities associated with land development and construction are required to obtain a stormwater permit if one-half (1/2) acre or more will be disturbed, or the construction is part of a Larger Common Plan (LCP)." The manual's own definition (Sec. 1, item 16) is: "Impervious Surface: a surface which has been compacted or covered with a layer of material so that it is highly resistant to infiltration by water. The term includes most conventionally surfaced streets, roofs, sidewalks, parking lots, and other similar structures." The manual contains NO mention of artificial turf, synthetic turf or synthetic grass anywhere in its 134 pages. It also requires, for sites without an existing outlet, that infiltration practices "accept, at a minimum, the first inch of runoff from all impervious areas," with post-development discharge limited to that of an equivalent site at SCS Curve Number 39.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Half an acre (21,780 sq ft) is the line that separates a residential job from a permitted project. A municipal softball field is well over it — a single full-size softball outfield alone is roughly an acre. So every municipal sports field job he chases will be a permitted stormwater project with engineered drainage, not a landscape install. That is a completely different bid, a different insurance posture, and requires a design professional. The CN 39 predevelopment benchmark is aggressive and is what his engineer will have to design to.
findings.confidence: high on content — retrieved and text-extracted in full; NOTE horrycountysc.gov was unreachable from this network today (connection refused), so the document was retrieved from the Internet Archive capture dated 2026-04-15 of that exact URL

findings.fact: South Carolina's general contractor licence threshold is $10,000, and turf installation falls inside the statutory definition of general construction. SC Code Ann. Sec. 40-11-30: "No entity or individual may practice as a contractor by performing or offering to perform contracting work for which the total cost of construction is greater than ten thousand dollars for general contracting or greater than ten thousand dollars for mechanical contracting without a license issued in accordance with this chapter." Sec. 40-11-20(10): "General construction means the installation, replacement, or repair of a building, structure, highway, sewer, grading, asphalt or concrete paving, or improvement of any kind to real property." Sec. 40-11-410 includes a Grading subclassification covering "soil preparation and rehabilitation of streets, roads, highways, railroad beds, building sites, parking lots, and storm sewers." There is NO landscaping classification anywhere in Chapter 40-11.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The widely repeated "$5,000 landscaping threshold" that appears on contractor-licensing SEO sites is wrong for this chapter — the statutory number is $10,000. Turf installation is "improvement of any kind to real property," and the excavation/base work maps onto the Grading subclassification. Because there is no landscaping category, an installer who wants unambiguous standing on jobs over $10,000 — which is most putting greens and every commercial job — is looking at a General Contractor licence, likely with a Grading subclassification. This is worth a call to LLR to confirm classification, because the answer determines whether he can legally bid municipal sports fields at all.
findings.confidence: high on the statutory text; medium on which subclassification LLR would actually require — confirm with the Board

findings.fact: A separate and much lower threshold applies to residential work under the Residential Builders Commission. SC Code Ann. Sec. 40-59-20 defines a "Residential builder" as one who constructs or superintends construction, repair or improvement of a residential building "when the cost of the undertaking exceeds five thousand dollars," and a "Residential specialty contractor" as "an independent contractor who contracts with a licensed residential builder, general contractor, or individual property owner to do construction work, repairs, improvement, or reimprovement which requires special skills and involves the use of specialized construction trades or craft, when the undertakings exceed five hundred dollars." The enumerated specialty trades are plumbers, electricians, HVAC, siding, insulation, roofing, floor covering, masonry, drywall, carpentry, stucco, painting/wallpaper and solar panel installers — landscaping is NOT among them. Sec. 40-59-220 requires residential builders to be licensed and residential specialty contractors to be registered; residential builders need a minimum $15,000 surety bond, and specialty contractors doing work over $5,000 for individual property owners need a bond in a Commission-approved amount.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Two thresholds, two different boards, and turf sits in the gap. Because landscaping is named in neither Chapter 40-11 nor the 40-59 specialty list, the licensing status of a residential turf install in SC is genuinely ambiguous — which is exactly why he should get a written classification determination from LLR rather than rely on what a competitor tells him. The $500 specialty threshold is low enough that if LLR treats turf as a residential specialty trade, essentially every job he does needs registration.
findings.confidence: high on statutory text; the gap in coverage for landscaping/turf is a real ambiguity, not a drafting oversight I can resolve from the code alone

findings.fact: South Carolina LLR's public licence verification portal is at https://verify.llronline.com/LicLookup/ (the search page is LookupMain.aspx, with a Contractors board search at /Contractors/Contractor.aspx). This is the site a Horry County homeowner would use to check whether an installer holds a current SC contractor licence or residential builder licence.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: He should put this link on his own site next to his licence number. In a market this saturated with unlicensed operators, inviting the customer to verify you is a conversion asset, not a risk. It also arms his commercial clients — a municipality will verify before award regardless.

The URL is confirmed by Internet Archive captures returning HTTP 200 in Jan 2025, and archived captures show LLR reorganised its site during 2025-2026 with old /POL/Contractors paths now returning 404. findings.fact: No jurisdiction in the South Carolina half of the service area has any ordinance that names artificial turf, synthetic turf, artificial grass or synthetic grass — neither restricting nor permitting it. Searched in full text: Horry County Code Chapter 17.7 (Stormwater, all three articles) and Appendix B Zoning Articles IV (General Provisions), V (Landscape/Buffer/Tree Protection), VII (Parking), IX (Conditional Uses), XIV (Glossary); Myrtle Beach Code Chapter 18 (Stormwater, complete) and Appendix A Zoning Articles 2 (Definitions), 9 (Landscaping and Tree Protection), 10 (Parking), 11 (Floodplain), 13 (Supplemental Provisions), 14 (Zoning Districts), 15 (Conditional and Accessory Uses), 16 (Area/Height/Dimensional), 17 (Design and Performance Standards); North Myrtle Beach Code Chapter 13 (Stormwater) and Chapter 23 Zoning Articles I, V (Landscaping) and VII (General Supplementary, incl. Sec. 23-129 series); plus the Horry County Stormwater Management Design Manual (2024). Every occurrence of the word "turf" in these codes refers to live turf grass.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The regulatory risk here is not prohibition — it is silence. Nobody has written a rule saying turf is allowed, and nobody has written one saying it is banned, so each permit is decided by a staff member applying a general impervious-surface definition to a product the definition was not written for. That means outcomes vary by reviewer and by jurisdiction, and it means being the installer who arrives with infiltration test data and a drainage detail is a structural advantage. It also means he should not put "approved" or "code compliant" language on his site — there is nothing to be approved under.
findings.confidence: high for Horry County, Myrtle Beach and North Myrtle Beach (zoning and stormwater articles retrieved with full text). Lower for Conway and Surfside Beach — those codes were retrieved only at chapter level and their zoning article bodies were not fully expanded, so treat those two as unverified rather than confirmed-clear.

findings.fact: Both Horry County and Myrtle Beach require required landscape areas to be live plantings with irrigation, which forecloses turf in those specific areas. Horry County Zoning Appendix B, Article V: "Irrigation. a) Plantings must be mechanically irrigated." (with a limited exception for vehicle-use areas under 30 spaces, which still require a hose bib within 100 feet, and a warranty-bond alternative for residential developments using native drought-tolerant material). Myrtle Beach Zoning Sec. 902 requires that buffer areas "be seeded or sodded with a high-grade turf that will withstand the local climatic conditions" and that "In-ground irrigation shall be installed and proper operation maintained to support and sustain all the landscape material." Myrtle Beach also requires that "All newly landscaped areas shall have in-ground irrigation."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: On a commercial site the code-required buffers and parking-lot islands must be living, irrigated plant material — he cannot bid turf into those square feet. What is available to him is everything outside the required landscape areas: courtyards, play areas, pet runs, common lawns, entry features, rooftop terraces. He needs to read the approved landscape plan before quoting a commercial job so he does not price square footage that legally cannot be turf.

findings.fact: South Carolina's Homeowners Association Act (SC Code Title 27, Chapter 30) is purely procedural and places NO substantive limit on what landscaping or architectural restrictions an HOA may impose. It contains no mention of artificial turf, synthetic turf, drought-tolerant landscaping or xeriscaping. Its operative provisions are: Sec. 27-30-130, requiring governing documents to be recorded in the county Register of Deeds/RMC to be enforceable, and requiring rules and regulations to be re-recorded annually by January 10 to remain enforceable; Sec. 27-30-160, giving magistrates court concurrent jurisdiction over monetary disputes; and Sec. 27-30-340, requiring the Department of Consumer Affairs to collect complaints and publish an annual report. Title 27's chapter list confirms the only association-related chapters are Ch. 30 (Homeowners Associations) and Ch. 31 (Horizontal Property Act) — there is no SC statute protecting a homeowner's right to install synthetic turf, unlike Florida, Texas, Arizona and Nevada.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: In South Carolina the HOA wins. If the covenants ban artificial turf, there is no state law to override them — so architectural committee approval is a real gate on residential work, not a formality. Two practical consequences: (1) build ARC submittal support into the sales process (spec sheets, drainage detail, product samples, photos of approved neighbouring installs) because that is where deals die; (2) the annual January 10 re-recording requirement in Sec. 27-30-130 is a genuine lever — a rule that was never properly recorded may not be enforceable, which is worth a homeowner asking their attorney about when an ARC refuses.

findings.fact: South Carolina has 7,600 community associations containing 593,000 housing units and 1,419,000 residents — roughly a quarter of the state's population lives under an association. SC ranks 16th nationally by association count (national total 373,000). Source is the Foundation for Community Association Research 2025 Statistical Review, table "Community Associations by State."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Quantifies the ARC-approval problem. Combined with the fact that SC law gives homeowners no statutory protection, and that the Grand Strand's residential stock is unusually HOA-heavy (master-planned communities like Carolina Forest, Barefoot Resort, Grande Dunes, Market Common), HOA approval is likely the single biggest friction point in his residential funnel. A page on his site titled something like "Getting your HOA to approve artificial turf in Horry County" would capture real search intent and pre-solve the objection.
findings.confidence: high for the state figure. No county-level HOA count for Horry County was found — see not_found.

findings.fact: Grand Strand Water & Sewer Authority currently has a drought policy in effect that is VOLUNTARY, not mandatory, and that raises the cost of heavy outdoor water use. GSWSA's drought management policy update, effective July 1, 2026, was triggered by the South Carolina State Climatology Office declaring a severe drought condition for the Pee Dee River Basin (Horry, Marion and Dillon Counties). It states "Any irrigation use should occur outside the hours of 6:00 – 9:00 a.m." and "We request our customers to reduce/eliminate all non-essential water usage to protect our service area during this time." Critically, it moves the excess-usage billing threshold down: "excess charges will begin after 6,000 gallons of usage" (from the normal 8,000). Separately, GSWSA's standing Smart Irrigation guidance asks customers to "Skip Irrigating on Mondays," to water by house number (odd numbers Tue/Thu/Sat, even numbers Wed/Fri/Sun), and to "Avoid Watering Between 6:00 AM and 9:00 AM."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is his strongest current water-conservation talking point and it is time-sensitive — a live severe-drought declaration in the county as of July 2026. The 8,000-to-6,000 gallon change is the sharpest number he has: a homeowner irrigating a lawn is now hitting excess charges 25% sooner. He can build a credible, checkable ROI argument on it. But he must present the odd/even schedule as guidance, not law — GSWSA's language is voluntary and he should not overstate it.

findings.fact: There is NO turf rebate, water rebate, or landscape-conversion incentive programme anywhere in the South Carolina service area. GSWSA's Smart Irrigation and Water Conservation Tips pages carry no rebate, no incentive and no irrigation-meter programme. Full-text search of the Horry County Code, the Myrtle Beach Code, the North Myrtle Beach Code and the Conway Code returned zero water-conservation rebate or landscape-conversion incentive provisions (the only "rebate" hits are tax-increment-financing and procurement-ethics provisions, unrelated). This is the opposite of the Southwest US market, where turf-for-grass rebates of $1–$3 per square foot are common and are a major part of the sales pitch.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: A genuinely useful negative. He must not import Arizona/Nevada/California marketing copy — any "ask about rebates" language on his site would be a false claim in this market and would burn trust on the first call. His water argument has to stand on the customer's own bill (see the GSWSA 6,000-gallon threshold above), not on a subsidy that does not exist here.
findings.confidence: high — searched the four municipal codes plus the water authority's public pages and found nothing; a programme could exist off-code, but nothing surfaced

findings.fact: Myrtle Beach has its own drought ordinance with mandatory teeth at the severe phase. Code Chapter 21, Article VI (Sec. 21-125 et seq.), adopted under the South Carolina Drought Response Act of 2000 (SC Code Sec. 49-23-10 et seq.), establishes four drought alert phases (incipient, moderate, severe, extreme). At the moderate phase measures are voluntary, targeting a 10% reduction and asking customers to "Reduce watering of lawns, plants, trees, gardens, shrubbery and flora on private or public property to the minimum necessary." At the SEVERE phase the city moves to "mandatory restrictions on non-essential usage and restrictions on times when certain water usage is allowed," targeting a 20% reduction, and will "Control landscape irrigation by the utility's customers by staggering watering times." Conway (Title 4, Chapter 4) and North Myrtle Beach (Sec. 15-93/15-94) have parallel drought management and response ordinances.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Unlike GSWSA's voluntary request, this is enforceable municipal law that switches on automatically when the state drought committee escalates. Given that the Pee Dee basin was already declared in severe drought as of mid-2026, the phase escalation is a live risk his customers can feel. This is legitimate, sourced material for the water argument — and it applies to commercial customers (hotels, HOAs, daycares) whose irrigation bills and reputational exposure are larger than a homeowner's.

findings.fact: Horry County is one of the most repeatedly flood-declared counties on the East Coast. FEMA's OpenFEMA disaster declaration data lists Horry County (SC) as a designated area in major disaster or emergency declarations for Hurricane Matthew (2016/2017), Severe Storms and Flooding (2016, DR-4241), Hurricane Irma (2017/2018), Hurricane Florence (2018, DR-4394 and EM-3400), Hurricane Dorian (2019), Hurricane Ian (2022 and 2023), Hurricane Idalia (2023), Tropical Storm/Hurricane Debby (2024) and Hurricane Helene (2024). FEMA's NFIP redacted claims dataset records 12,523 flood insurance claims for county code 45051 (Horry County, SC), and 439,769 NFIP policy records for the county (dataset frozen 2026-06-01).
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Seven named-storm declarations in nine years is the operating environment, not an edge case. It has three commercial consequences: (1) his base and drainage design has to survive inundation and lateral water movement, not just rainfall percolation — a turf system that floats, migrates or silts up after one storm surge is a warranty disaster; (2) "drains faster than sod and doesn't wash out" is a stronger local sales argument here than water savings; (3) municipal and school sports-field buyers in this county care more about how fast a field is playable after a storm than about anything else, which is precisely the case for synthetic fields and is his best commercial wedge.
findings.confidence: high — queried directly against FEMA's OpenFEMA API today

findings.fact: In Myrtle Beach's Coastal High Hazard (VE) flood zones, the compacted aggregate base used in a standard turf installation is effectively prohibited. Zoning Sec. 1111.F: "There shall be no fill used as structural support. Limited non-compacted fill may be used around the perimeter of a building for landscaping/aesthetic purposes provided the fill will wash out from storm surge, thereby rendering the building free of obstruction prior to generating loading forces, ramping effects or wave deflection. Only beach compatible sand may be used. The local administrator shall approve design plans for landscaping/aesthetic fill only after the applicant has provided an analysis by an engineer, architect, and/or soil scientist which demonstrates that the following factors have been fully considered: 1. Particle composition of fill material does not have a tendency for excessive natural compaction; 2. Volume and distribution of fill will not cause wave deflection to adjacent properties; and, 3. Slope of fill will not cause wave run-up or ramping." Sec. 1111.G adds: "There shall be no alteration of sand dunes which would increase potential flood damage." Sec. 1112.C limits fill on all oceanfront lots to 2–3 ft above existing grade. In AE zones, Sec. 1110 requires fill to be "compatible with the existing soils."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Three separate clauses in this one section — no compacted fill, fill must wash out in a surge, and only beach-compatible sand — each independently rule out a conventional crushed-stone turf base on an oceanfront VE-zone lot. This matters commercially because oceanfront Myrtle Beach and North Myrtle Beach properties are exactly the high-budget residential and hospitality jobs he would most want. He needs either a sand-based install detail engineered for VE zones, or a clear internal rule that VE-zone lots are a no-bid. Either way, he should be checking the flood zone before quoting anything east of Ocean Boulevard.

findings.fact: South Carolina's child care licensing regulations (SC Code of Regulations Chapter 114, Department of Social Services) govern playground surfacing but do not name synthetic turf. The standards require: "Stationary outdoor equipment shall be firmly anchored and shall not be placed on a concrete or asphalt surface. Cushioning material such as mats, wood chips or sand shall be used under climbers, slides, swings, and large pieces of equipment," and "Cushioning material shall extend at least six (6) feet beyond the equipment and swings." Equipment must also "Meet the standards of the U.S. Consumer Products Safety Commission (CPSC), if applicable."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Directly relevant to the daycare segment the owner wants. The regulation is open-ended — "cushioning material such as mats" — so a turf system over a certified shock pad is a plausible compliant surface, but it is not named, meaning the DSS licensing inspector decides. The commercially defensible move is to install to CPSC/ASTM F1292 critical-fall-height ratings for the equipment on site and hand the daycare operator the test documentation, so their licensing inspection passes on paper. Selling "we keep your DSS inspection clean" is a much stronger daycare pitch than aesthetics. Note the 6-foot fall-zone extension requirement drives square footage — quote it.
findings.confidence: medium-high — regulation text extracted verbatim from the official SC Statehouse PDF of Chapter 114, but the exact subsection number could not be pinned from the extracted text layout; cite the chapter, and confirm the section number before using it in a client-facing document

No SC statute limits what landscaping restrictions an HOA may impose. SC Code Title 27 contains only Chapter 30 (Homeowners Associations) and Chapter 31 (Horizontal Property Act); neither addresses landscaping, xeriscaping, drought-tolerant planting or synthetic turf. South Carolina has no equivalent to Florida's or Texas's statutory protections for water-conserving landscaping. Confirmed by reading both the Title 27 chapter index and the full text of Chapter 30.

The owner's core commercial claim — that Myrtle Beach is converting its municipal softball fields to synthetic turf — was NOT verified. cityofmyrtlebeach.com returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl, and myrtlebeachparksandrec.com was unreachable. The North Myrtle Beach Park & Sports Complex page was retrieved and contains no mention of turf. No procurement notice, bid solicitation, capital project or council agenda item confirming any municipal synthetic-turf field project in Horry County was found. Treat the claim as unverified market intelligence until a bid record or council minute is produced — this materially affects whether the commercial strategy is real.

Conway and Surfside Beach zoning provisions were retrieved only at chapter level; their zoning article bodies did not expand, so the 'no artificial turf ordinance' conclusion is UNVERIFIED for those two towns specifically (it is verified for Horry County, Myrtle Beach and North Myrtle Beach). Loris, Aynor, Atlantic Beach and Briarcliffe Acres were not searched at all beyond confirming Briarcliffe Acres has a Municode-published code.

Whether a properly built permeable turf system qualifies for the Horry County stormwater service-charge credit under Sec. 17.7-18 is NOT established. The ordinance authorises a credit for on-site detention/retention facilities per the county's 'stormwater utility service charge credit manual,' but that manual is hosted on the unreachable county site and was not obtained. Do not represent this credit to any client until the manual is read.

No SC Department of Environmental Services (formerly DHEC) guidance on artificial turf and the state NPDES construction general permit (SCR100000/SCR030000) was located. The Horry manual cross-references SCR030000 Section 4.2.4 but the state permit itself was not retrieved, so any state-level position on turf as impervious is unknown.

Web search quota for this session was exhausted after two queries, so all remaining research was done by fetching primary sources at known URLs (SC Statehouse, Municode API, FEMA OpenFEMA, GSWSA, CAI Foundation, Internet Archive). layer: North Carolina / Brunswick County regulatory layer for artificial turf installation
applies_to: The North Carolina portion of the service area: Brunswick County (unincorporated), Shallotte, Carolina Shores, Sunset Beach, Ash, Pireway, Longwood, Reeves, Calabash, Ocean Isle Beach and Holden Beach. Contrasted throughout against Horry County SC (Little River, Loris, Longs, North Myrtle Beach, Conway, Myrtle Beach).

findings.fact: North Carolina requires a state Landscape Contractor license from the NC Landscape Contractors' Licensing Board (NCLCLB) to "engage in the practice of landscape construction or contracting" or to use the designation "landscape contractor" or advertise in a way implying licensure (G.S. 89D-12(a)). The exemption threshold is at G.S. 89D-13(5): the Chapter does not apply to "Any landscaping work where the price of all contracts for labor, material, and other items for a given job site during any consecutive 12-month period is less than thirty thousand dollars ($30,000)." The same subdivision adds: "A local governmental unit shall not enact a local ordinance or regulation requiring licensure for landscaping work performed pursuant to this subdivision."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the single biggest cross-border difference for the business. A residential putting green or backyard turf lawn under $30,000 per job site (rolling 12 months) needs NO state license in NC. Above $30,000 the owner must be NCLCLB-licensed. Note the trap: the threshold is per JOB SITE over any consecutive 12-month period, so two $18,000 phases at the same house 10 months apart crosses it. South Carolina has no landscape contractor license at all, so an installer who has been working Horry County unlicensed can cross into Shallotte and unknowingly break NC law on a single mid-size commercial job.

findings.fact: North Carolina has a written, board-adopted workmanship standard specifically for artificial turf: 21 NCAC 28B .0503(b) — "When installing artificial turf, the licensed contractor shall: (1) Ensure that the sub-grade is compacted and shall pitch properly to drain; (2) Establish a perimeter attachment system to secure the artificial turf; (3) Roll out the turf with the nap facing a consistent direction; (4) Secure the turf with an evenly weighted sand layer distributed over the entire surface; and (5) Follow all manufacturer's specifications for the type of turf being installed." Rule effective September 1, 2016, amended July 1, 2021.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: North Carolina is one of very few states with artificial turf installation written into its licensing rules. Two consequences: (1) it is marketing gold — "installed to the North Carolina Landscape Contractors' Licensing Board standard, 21 NCAC 28B .0503(b)" is a checkable claim no Myrtle Beach competitor can make, because South Carolina has no equivalent rule; (2) it is an enforcement hook — a licensed installer who skips the perimeter attachment system or the sand ballast has violated a board rule and is exposed to discipline and civil penalty. It also means NC counter staff and inspectors have a written reference for what a correct turf install looks like.

findings.fact: North Carolina General Statute 143-214.7D(b)(6), enacted by S.L. 2024-49 s. 4.48(b), states that for purposes of implementing State or local government stormwater programs, the following shall NOT be considered built-upon area or an impervious or partially impervious surface: "Artificial turf, manufactured to allow water to drain through the backing of the turf, and installed according to the manufacturer's specifications over a pervious surface." Subsection (c) lets an owner/developer opt out of the exemption. The same section also exempts slatted decks, pool water area, #57 stone at least four inches thick over geotextile fabric, qualifying trails, and landscaping material including gravel, mulch and sand.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the most commercially valuable fact in the whole NC layer. Under state law, correctly specified and installed drainable artificial turf over a pervious base counts as ZERO built-upon area in North Carolina. On a Brunswick County commercial site — a daycare, a pet daycare, a municipal ball field — that means turf does not eat the project's impervious budget, does not push it from low-density into high-density stormwater design, and does not force additional engineered stormwater controls. That is a direct, quantifiable cost argument to a developer or a town parks department. The two conditions are load-bearing: the turf must be manufactured to drain through the backing, and it must be installed per manufacturer spec over a pervious surface. Keep the manufacturer's drainage-rate cut sheet and an installation certification in every commercial file.

findings.fact: G.S. 143-214.7D(d): "Except as specifically required by federal law, a local government may not enact, implement, or enforce a local government ordinance, comprehensive plan, or stormwater program that establishes a definition of 'built-upon area' or impervious surface that does not comply with subsection (b) of this section. This limitation shall apply regardless of any authority granted by G.S. 143-214.5, G.S. 143-214.7, or Chapters 153A, 160A, or 160D of the General Statutes." The bill that created it (H426 committee substitute, 2024) also directed at Section 3(c): "Each unit of local government that operates a stormwater program shall update its program to be consistent with G.S. 143-214.7D."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the client's answer when a Brunswick County, Shallotte or Sunset Beach counter clerk says "turf counts as impervious here." State law expressly preempts a local definition that conflicts. It converts a project-killing objection into a 10-minute conversation with a citation. Every commercial and residential quote in NC should carry this citation on the back page.

findings.fact: Brunswick County's own Stormwater Quality Management and Discharge Control Ordinance (the current PDF the County links from its Stormwater Ordinance page) defines built-upon area at Section 1.5(d) as: "Impervious surface and partially impervious surface to the extent that the partially impervious surface does not allow water to infiltrate through the surface and into the subsoil. BUA does not include a slatted wood deck or the water area of a swimming pool; a surface of number 57 stone... laid at least four inches thick over a geotextile fabric; or a trail as defined in G.S. 113A-85..." It does NOT list artificial turf, and does not list landscaping material such as gravel or mulch. The County's Municode-published Code Sec. 1-13-196 is worse still, defining built-upon area to expressly INCLUDE "gravel areas such as roads, parking lots, and paths" — and that Municode publication is only codified through Ordinance UDO-21-01 adopted May 17, 2021 (Supp. No. 26).
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Brunswick County's written stormwater definitions are behind the 2024 statute. Expect real friction at the County Stormwater Administrator's desk, because the reviewer's own ordinance text omits the turf exemption. The fix is not to argue but to lead with G.S. 143-214.7D(b)(6) and (d), plus the manufacturer's drainage spec. Also budget schedule time: an out-of-date local ordinance means a first-of-its-kind review, not a routine one.

findings.fact: Brunswick County Stormwater Ordinance Section 1.16(b) requires a Stormwater Management Plan approved by the Stormwater Administrator, and therefore a Brunswick County Stormwater Permit, for: (i) all non-residential development and any major subdivision; (ii) any activity that disturbs land within 30 feet of the banks of a stream or other natural waterway; (iii) "Any filling or excavation of a parcel that results in a change of land surface of four (4) inches or more and alters the existing drainage pattern" (with a narrow septic-system carve-out); and (iv) any activity or development ultimately disturbing one or more acres. The County UDO Section 3.9.1 cross-references the same permit.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: A typical turf install strips 3–4 inches of sod and lays 3–4 inches of aggregate base. That is squarely inside the "four inches or more" excavation/fill trigger, and every commercial job (daycare, pet daycare, ballfield) is caught by clause (i) regardless of size. So in unincorporated Brunswick County, a commercial turf project needs a County stormwater permit as a matter of course, and even a residential job can trip the four-inch trigger if it alters drainage. In Horry County SC there is no analogous four-inch grading trigger at the county level for a small residential landscape job. Price the permit time into every NC bid.

findings.fact: Brunswick County is one of North Carolina's 20 statutory "Coastal Counties" (15A NCAC 02H .1002(6), which names Beaufort, Bertie, Brunswick, Camden, Carteret, Chowan, Craven, Currituck, Dare, Gates, Hertford, Hyde, New Hanover, Onslow, Pamlico, Pasquotank, Pender, Perquimans, Tyrrell, Washington). Under 15A NCAC 02H .1019, the coastal stormwater rule applies to projects requiring an erosion and sedimentation control plan, projects requiring a CAMA Major Development Permit, and otherwise to non-residential projects cumulatively adding 10,000 sq ft or more of built-upon area (or residential projects within 1/2 mile of and draining to SA waters adding more than 10,000 sq ft of BUA and exceeding 12% BUA). Maximum BUA for the low-density option is 12% near SA waters and freshwater ORW, and 24% for other coastal county waters; anything above that is "high density" and must treat the 1.5-inch storm (or the one-year, 24-hour storm near SA waters).
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Those low-density caps are brutally tight — 24% built-upon on a commercial parcel, 12% near shellfish waters. A daycare playground, a pet-daycare run yard or a municipal ballfield made of concrete or conventional paving would blow the budget. Because G.S. 143-214.7D(b)(6) zeroes out qualifying artificial turf, the client can honestly pitch turf as the surface that keeps a Brunswick County site under the low-density threshold and out of engineered stormwater controls entirely. This is the strongest commercial sales argument available on the NC side of the line, and it does not exist in Horry County SC because SC has no coastal-county BUA cap of this kind.

findings.fact: CAMA applies only inside a designated Area of Environmental Concern. G.S. 113A-103(5)a defines "development" as "any activity in a duly designated area of environmental concern... involving, requiring, or consisting of the construction or enlargement of a structure; excavation; dredging; filling; dumping; removal of clay, silt, sand, gravel or minerals; bulkheading, driving of pilings; clearing or alteration of land as an adjunct of construction; alteration or removal of sand dunes; alteration of the shore, bank, or bottom..." G.S. 113A-118(a) requires a CAMA permit before undertaking any development in an AEC, in addition to any other State or local permit. Under 113A-118(d), a "major development" is one requiring another State or federal permit, or occupying more than 20 acres, or drilling/excavating natural resources, or occupying on a single parcel structures exceeding 60,000 sq ft of ground area; a "minor development" is everything else, permitted by the local CAMA permit officer.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the precise CAMA answer the client needs. A turf installation is not automatically a CAMA matter — the trigger is LOCATION, not activity. But once the work sits inside an AEC, the excavation, filling and land alteration inherent in a turf base absolutely fall inside the statutory definition of "development," so a CAMA minor development permit is required before the first shovel. Practical rule for the crew: on any Sunset Beach, Ocean Isle Beach or Holden Beach oceanfront or waterfront lot, and on any lot within 75 feet of an estuarine shoreline anywhere in Brunswick County, call the local CAMA permit officer BEFORE scheduling. Note also that a Brunswick County site needing a CAMA Major Permit is automatically pulled into the coastal stormwater rule under 15A NCAC 02H .1019(2)(b).

findings.fact: 15A NCAC 07H .0209(a) sets the Coastal Shorelines AEC boundaries: estuarine shorelines AEC extend 75 feet landward from normal high water/normal water level; where the estuarine shoreline is immediately contiguous to Outstanding Resource Waters, the AEC extends 575 feet landward; public trust shorelines AEC extend 30 feet landward. Within that AEC, 07H .0209(d)(2) provides: "All development projects, proposals, and designs shall limit the construction of impervious surfaces and areas not allowing natural drainage to only so much as is necessary to service the primary purpose or use for which the lot is to be developed. Impervious surfaces shall not exceed 30 percent of the AEC area of the lot, unless the applicant can demonstrate, through innovative design, that the protection provided by the design would be equal to or exceed the protection by the 30 percent limitation." 07H .0209(d)(10) additionally requires new development to sit 30 feet landward of normal water level, with a listed exception at (d)(10)(G) for "Grading, excavation and landscaping with no wetland fill... Projects shall not increase stormwater runoff to adjacent estuarine and public trust waters."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Two things. First, the 30% AEC impervious cap is a separate, tighter constraint from the county stormwater rules, measured only over the portion of the lot inside the AEC — a waterfront Sunset Beach lot can be maxed out before the homeowner even starts. Second, and importantly, note the wording: 07H uses "impervious surfaces," and G.S. 143-214.7D(b) is written "for the purposes of implementing State or local government stormwater programs." Whether the turf exemption reaches a Coastal Resources Commission AEC rule is a genuine open question — do not assume it does. The safe play on an AEC lot is the (d)(10)(G) landscaping exception plus a written demonstration that the installation does not increase runoff to adjacent waters.

findings.fact: For oceanfront property, 15A NCAC 07H .0306(a)(2) states the ocean hazard setback is determined by both development size and the shoreline long-term erosion rate, and expressly says: "'Development size' is defined by total floor area for structures and buildings or total area of footprint for development other than structures and buildings." The setback ladder at .0306(a)(3) runs from 60 feet or 30x the erosion rate (under 5,000 sq ft) to 120 feet or 60x (5,000–10,000 sq ft), 130 feet or 65x (10,000–20,000 sq ft), and upward; parking lots of 5,000 sq ft or more get 120 feet or 60x.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: On Sunset Beach or Holden Beach oceanfront, a large turf installation is "development other than structures and buildings" and is measured by FOOTPRINT. A 6,000 sq ft turf area could therefore be argued into the 120-foot / 60x-erosion-rate setback band rather than the 60-foot band. This is a size-driven cliff that a Horry County SC installer would never encounter. On oceanfront lots, size the installation deliberately and confirm the setback band with the CAMA local permit officer before quoting.

findings.fact: 15A NCAC 07K lists the activities in AECs that do NOT require a CAMA permit. Notably, 07K .0101 adopts the statutory exclusions from "development" in G.S. 113A-103(5)(b)(1)-(9); 07K .0208 exempts single-family residences constructed in the Coastal Shorelines AEC more than 40 feet landward of normal high water where there is no land disturbance in the 40-foot buffer (and requires that notification to the CAMA local permit officer include "the dimensions of the proposed project, including proposed landscaping"); and 07K .0209 exempts certain accessory uses and maintenance/repair/replacement, subject to criteria including that the development "must not disturb a land area of greater than 200 square feet on a slope of greater than 10 percent" and "must not alter naturally or artificially created surface drainage channels."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: There is no blanket "landscaping is exempt from CAMA" rule — that is a common and dangerous assumption. The exemptions are narrow and several of them require advance notification to the local permit officer so an on-site review can happen. Note that 07K .0208(d)(2) specifically expects the notification to describe proposed landscaping, which is the hook a permit officer will use to ask about a turf area. Treat every AEC job as requiring a pre-work call.

findings.fact: The Town of Shallotte Unified Development Ordinance (adopted July 2004, amendments through April 2026, PDF dated 2026-03-24) defines Impervious Surface at (126) and again in its stormwater definitions as: "Any surface which in whole or in part, restricts or prevents the natural absorption of water into the ground. Such surfaces may include, but not be limited to, compacted earth (such as marl and coquina), gravel, concrete, asphalt, or other paving material, and all area covered by the footprint of buildings or structures. Uncovered wooden slatted decks and the water area of a swimming pool are considered pervious." Its Built-upon Area definition covers "that portion of a development project that is covered by impervious or partially impervious cover including buildings, pavement, gravel roads, and recreation facilities." Neither definition mentions artificial turf, #57 stone, trails, or landscaping material.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Shallotte amended this ordinance in 2026 and still has not conformed the definition to G.S. 143-214.7D. Worse for the client, its BUA definition expressly sweeps in "recreation facilities" — a phrase a reviewer could reach for on a putting green or sports field. Expect this to be the hardest of the four NC jurisdictions to get a clean turf-is-not-BUA determination from, and go in with the statute and the preemption subsection (d) in hand.

findings.fact: Shallotte UDO Section 25-15(B) requires a Stormwater Management Plan and Town Stormwater Permit for: (1) all commercial and industrial and other non-residential development and any major subdivision; (2) any activity disturbing land within 30 feet of the banks of a stream or natural waterway; (3) "Any filling or excavation of a parcel that results in a change of land surface that increases stormwater runoff onto adjacent parcels"; and (4) any activity or development ultimately disturbing one acre or more, OR ten thousand (10,000) square feet or more of impervious surfaces. Section 3.9 lists the other approvals a Shallotte zoning permit is conditioned on, including Town stormwater permit, Town floodplain permit, NCDENR stormwater permit, NCDENR soil & erosion control permit, NCDENR CAMA permit, NCDOT driveway permit and Brunswick County septic permit.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Any commercial turf job inside Shallotte town limits — and Shallotte is the commercial hub of the NC side of the territory — triggers a Town stormwater permit automatically. Build that into the schedule and the price. The runoff-onto-adjacent-parcels trigger at (3) is also a live risk on tight residential lots.

findings.fact: The Town of Sunset Beach UDO defines Impervious Surface as: "Any surface which in whole or in part, restricts or prevents the natural absorption of water into the ground. Such surfaces may include, but not be limited to compacted earth (such as marl and coquina), gravel, concrete, concrete pavers, asphalt, or other paving material, and all areas covered by the footprint of buildings or structures. The following are considered pervious surfaces: uncovered wooden slatted decks; the water area of a swimming pool; a surface of number 57 stone... laid at least four inches thick over a geotextile fabric (needle punched, non-woven, high survivability, with a puncture strength of 250 newtons); or a trail as defined in GS 143B-135.94B that is either unpaved or paved as long as the pavement is porous with a hydraulic conductivity greater than 0.001 centimeters per second (1.41 inches per hour)." Critically, it then adds: "Alternative materials, not subject to the definition of impervious surface, may be proposed subject to certification of a licensed and certified North Carolina professional engineer of compliance with the hydraulic conductivity standard of 1.41 inches per hour or greater. Such certification shall be in the form of a letter under seal."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Sunset Beach's list tracks the OLD pre-2024 statute — it has #57 stone and trails but not artificial turf and not landscaping material. But Sunset Beach is the only one of the four NC jurisdictions that gives the client a clean, written path that does not require arguing preemption: get a sealed letter from a North Carolina PE certifying the turf assembly's hydraulic conductivity at 1.41 in/hr or greater, and the town's own ordinance says it is not impervious. Build a standing relationship with one NC-licensed PE, get a template letter for the client's standard turf assembly, and this becomes a repeatable, low-friction approval. That is a competitive moat.

findings.fact: Sunset Beach UDO Section 2.13(B) and (C) and Section 2.12(B): a zoning permit is required for, among other things, "any activity which proposes to increase the amount of impervious square footage on a lot," and it is unlawful to commence "the paving, site disturbance, tree removal, or other installation or construction of a hardened surface upon the site" before the UDO Administrator issues that permit. A stormwater management plan is required prior to issuance of any permit for new construction or renovation/expansion "where the impervious surface coverage increases by greater than 200 square feet," and those plans must be designed by a professional engineer, registered landscape architect or licensed surveyor and inspected and approved after construction. Residential development may not exceed 45% impervious surface of total lot area; within the CR-1, CR-2 and AF-1 zoning districts not more than 20% of total lot area may be covered by impervious surfaces. A final as-built survey by a registered land surveyor must include impervious surface percentages, and "If the subject property is within a CAMA AEC, the survey must include information specific to the impervious surface percentage within the limits of the AEC."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the sharpest single illustration of the state-line contrast the client asked for. In Sunset Beach, a homeowner adding a 300 sq ft putting green faces: a zoning permit, a stormwater management plan sealed by a PE/RLA/surveyor, a post-construction inspection, an as-built survey stating impervious percentages, a 45% lot-wide cap, and — if the lot is in an AEC — a separate AEC-specific impervious percentage on that survey, plus a possible CAMA minor permit. Ten minutes away in Little River SC, the same 300 sq ft green is typically an unpermitted landscaping job with no state contractor license, no stormwater plan and no survey. The 200 sq ft threshold is the crux: almost every job the client sells clears it.

findings.fact: The Town of Carolina Shores issues its own Stormwater Permit on a town form that requires the applicant to state pre-development impervious area ("sq. feet of existing house, concrete, and any other structures on property"), the "Calculation of sq. feet to be added," and post-development impervious area. Its general notes state that a stormwater plan is required on all construction that ties into a Town-maintained stormwater facility, that "No increase in discharge is allowed into Town stormwater facilities," and that "No directional change in stormwater flow is permissible." Separately, the Town's Development Permit Application is the required cover application for all trade permits and must be completed for lot activity including "Clearing" and "Grading/Filling," and it asks for the contractor's "NC License #" and license expiration date.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Carolina Shores runs a lightweight but real permit regime that captures grading and filling — the exact activities in a turf base install — and its permit form asks for an NC license number on its face. A crew arriving from Horry County with no NC license number to write in the box will be stopped at the counter. Also note the absolute rules: no increase in discharge to town facilities and no directional change in flow. Turf's zero-BUA status under state law helps enormously with both, but the client will need to say so on the form.

findings.fact: South Carolina has no landscape contractor license. SC Code Title 40 Chapter 59 (Residential Builders Commission) lists the residential specialty contractor classifications at 40-59-20(7) as: plumbers; electricians; heating and air conditioning installers and repairers; vinyl and aluminum siding installers; insulation installers; roofers; floor covering installers; masons; dry wall installers; carpenters; stucco installers; painters and wall paperers; solar panel installers. Landscaping does not appear anywhere in Chapter 40-59, and the only occurrence of "landscape" in Title 40 Chapter 11 (Contractor's Licensing Board) is the reference to a licensed landscape architect as a "design professional." The SC thresholds are: residential builder license above $5,000 (40-59-20(6)); residential specialty contractor registration above $500 (40-59-20(7)) with a surety bond required when an undertaking for an individual property owner exceeds $5,000 (40-59-240(D)); and general or mechanical contractor license above $10,000, raised from $5,000 by 2023 Act No. 69 effective May 19, 2023 (40-11-30).
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The clean statement of the cross-border licensing difference: in South Carolina, artificial turf installation is not a licensed trade at the state level — there is no board, no exam, no bond, no workmanship rule. In North Carolina it is a licensed trade above $30,000 per job site, with an exam, a $10,000 bond, mandatory CE, and a written artificial-turf installation standard. That asymmetry is both a compliance obligation and a marketing asset: the client can hold an NC license that no SC-only competitor holds, and use it on both sides of the line as a credential.

findings.fact: NC license mechanics: G.S. 89D-16(a)(4) requires a $10,000 corporate surety bond or irrevocable letter of credit, maintained continuously, and any person injured by a licensee's violation may sue the licensee and the surety. G.S. 89D-20 requires renewal by August 1 each year and seven continuing education units per year; unrenewed licenses are automatically revoked. 21 NCAC 28B .0601 sets fees: Application $75, Examination $150, Individual license $100, Corporate license $100, Renewal $100, Late renewal $25, Reinstatement $100, License by reciprocity $100, Duplicate license $25. G.S. 89D-12(e) requires the license to be displayed at the place of business and the license number to appear "on all business cards, contracts, and vehicles used by the contractor in the landscape contracting business." G.S. 89D-19 permits licensure by reciprocity without examination where another state's requirements are substantially equivalent. License verification is public at the Board's search portal.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Total cost of entry is small — roughly $325 in board fees plus the bond — against the value of unlocking every NC job over $30,000 and every NC commercial job. But two operational items bite: reciprocity from South Carolina is effectively unavailable because SC has no landscape contractor license to be substantially equivalent to, so the owner must sit the NC exam (landscape design, general knowledge, and plant identification from photographs). And the vehicle-lettering requirement is a visible compliance item — NC trucks must carry the license number.

findings.fact: 21 NCAC 28B .0501(a) requires that services performed by a licensed NC landscape contractor exceeding $5,000 in value be described in a written agreement before work commences, containing at minimum: the business name, license number, business address and telephone number of the licensed contractor; the name and address of the client; the address or location of work if different; the date of the proposal; the description of the work; the total value in lump sum, unit price, or time and material price; the estimated time of completion; and the terms of payment.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Every NC turf job above $5,000 — which is essentially all of them — must be under a written contract with those specific elements, including the license number in the contract itself. South Carolina imposes no equivalent contract-content rule on landscaping work. The client should build one NC contract template that satisfies this rule and use it for every job north of the line.

findings.fact: G.S. 89D-12(c): "A landscape contractor licensed under this Chapter is not required to be licensed as a general contractor under Article 1 of Chapter 87 of the General Statutes if the licensed landscape contractor is performing landscape construction or contracting work valued at an amount greater than forty thousand dollars ($40,000)." G.S. 89D-13(6) separately exempts from Chapter 89D a licensed general contractor holding a building, residential or public utilities classification. North Carolina's general contractor threshold is $40,000, raised from $30,000 effective October 1, 2023.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the make-or-break provision for the commercial work the owner wants. Municipal ballfields, sports complexes and larger commercial installs run well past $40,000. Without an NCLCLB license, a turf installer bidding a $250,000 municipal field in North Carolina would be pushed into needing a full NC general contractor license (with its financial-statement and exam requirements). With the NCLCLB license, 89D-12(c) lets the client bid that work directly. Getting licensed is not paperwork — it is the gate to the commercial segment on the NC side.

findings.fact: A South Carolina company operating in North Carolina needs more than an individual license. G.S. 89D-17 requires the Board to issue a license in the name of a corporation or LLC only where one or more officers, managers, executives or full-time employees are individually licensed, only those persons execute NC landscape contracts, and they are "readily available to exercise supervision over the work performed." G.S. 89D-18(c) adds: "The Board shall not issue a license for a foreign corporation unless the corporation has obtained a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State... The Board shall not issue a license for a foreign limited liability company unless the company has obtained a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State pursuant to Article 7 of Chapter 57D." If the licensed individual leaves, the entity has 120 days to replace them or the entity license is automatically suspended and it must cease practicing.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: If Timeless Grass & Greens is an SC entity, crossing into NC properly is a three-step process, not one: register the entity with the NC Secretary of State for a certificate of authority, get the owner individually NCLCLB-licensed, and then get the entity a corporate NCLCLB license naming him. Skipping the certificate of authority blocks the entity license entirely. Start this early — the exam is offered at least twice a year and must be passed within one year of application approval.

findings.fact: North Carolina separately licenses irrigation contracting. G.S. 89D-12(b)(4) expressly says nothing in the landscape contractor chapter authorizes "The practice of irrigation contracting, as defined in G.S. 89G-1." G.S. 89G-3(5) exempts irrigation construction or contracting work "where the price of all contracts for labor, material, and other items for a given jobsite is less than two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500)." South Carolina has no state irrigation contractor license.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Turf installs routinely involve capping, rerouting or removing existing irrigation. In North Carolina that work is a separate licensed trade above $2,500 per job site, and the landscape contractor license does not cover it. On a large residential or commercial NC job where irrigation modification is a meaningful line item, either stay under $2,500 on the irrigation scope, sub it to an NC-licensed irrigation contractor, or pursue the 89G license. This is an easy, invisible violation to commit.

findings.fact: Enforcement in NC: G.S. 89D-23(a) lets the Board "assess a civil penalty not in excess of two thousand dollars ($2,000) for each violation of any section of this Chapter or the violation of any rules adopted by the Board." G.S. 89D-24(a) lets the Board seek injunctive relief in superior court against unlicensed practice, and 89D-24(b) requires a licensed landscape contractor to notify the Board by registered mail of any written complaint not resolved within 30 days of filing. G.S. 89D-22 lists grounds for denial, restriction, suspension or revocation including gross malpractice or incompetence and willful violation of Board rules.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Two exposures. First, unlicensed work above $30,000 in NC invites a civil penalty and an injunction. Second — and this is the one most contractors miss — the 30-day complaint-notification duty at 89D-24(b) is affirmative: an unresolved written customer complaint must be self-reported to the Board. Build that into the office process.

findings.fact: North Carolina HOAs are governed by the NC Planned Community Act, Chapter 47F. G.S. 47F-1-102(a) applies the Act to planned communities created on or after January 1, 1999, excluding communities of 20 lots or fewer and all-nonresidential communities. G.S. 47F-1-102(c) applies an enumerated subset of the Act — including 47F-3-102(1)-(6) and (11)-(17) (powers), 47F-3-107.1 (fine procedures), 47F-3-115 (assessments) and 47F-3-116 (liens) — to communities created BEFORE January 1, 1999 unless the articles or declaration expressly provide otherwise. G.S. 47F-3-102(12) empowers an association, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, to "impose reasonable fines or suspend privileges or services... for violations of the declaration, bylaws, and rules and regulations." G.S. 47F-3-107.1 caps a fine at one hundred dollars ($100.00) per violation and then permits $100 "for each day more than five days after the decision that the violation occurs," and provides that "Such fines shall be assessments secured by liens under G.S. 47F-3-116."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: NC gives an HOA teeth. A homeowner who installs turf without architectural review approval faces a hearing, then $100 per day, and those fines become a lien on the home enforceable under 47F-3-116. That is a real risk the client should manage rather than ignore: make written ARC approval a condition precedent in the NC contract, and get it in the file before mobilizing. Turning ARC submittals into a service the client performs for the customer is a genuine differentiator in the Brunswick beach towns.

findings.fact: North Carolina has no statute protecting a homeowner's right to install artificial turf against HOA restrictions. Chapter 47F's only landscaping-specific protection is G.S. 47F-3-122 ("Irrigation of landscaping"), which provides that notwithstanding any declaration of covenants, no requirement to irrigate landscaping shall be construed to require irrigation during a period when the U.S. Drought Monitor or the Secretary of Environmental Quality has designated the association's area as in severe, extreme or exceptional drought and a government has imposed water conservation measures — subject to detailed covenant-language exceptions — and it defines "landscaping" to include "lawns, trees, shrubbery, and other ornamental or decorative plants." Chapter 47F does contain express carve-outs for other things (47F-3-121 protects American and State flag and political sign displays), which underscores that artificial turf simply is not protected.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: An HOA in Sunset Beach, Carolina Shores or Calabash can lawfully ban artificial turf outright, and there is no NC statute to argue against it. The workable angle is 47F-3-122 by analogy in the sales conversation — the legislature has already recognized that drought and water-conservation orders should not force irrigation of lawns — plus a water-savings case to the board. But it is persuasion, not a legal right. Sell to HOA boards and ARCs directly rather than fighting them lot by lot.

findings.fact: HOA governance differs materially across the state line. South Carolina's Homeowners Association Act, S.C. Code 27-30-130, provides that to be enforceable a homeowners association's governing documents must be recorded in the county register of deeds/RMC office, and that "In order to remain enforceable, a homeowners association's rules, regulations, and amendments to rules and regulations must be recorded... by January tenth of each year following their adoption or amendment." S.C. Code 27-30-340 requires the SC Department of Consumer Affairs to receive and record data from homeowner and HOA calls and written complaints on a prescribed form. North Carolina's Chapter 47F contains no annual recording requirement for rules and regulations and creates no state agency to receive HOA complaints.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Concrete cross-border tactic. In Horry County SC, if an HOA cites an unrecorded rule banning artificial turf, the client can ask whether that rule was recorded by January 10 of the following year — an unrecorded rule is not enforceable under 27-30-130(B)(2). In Brunswick County NC there is no such check: an NC HOA's rules bind whether or not they were recorded annually, and there is no state complaint channel. Practically, this means NC HOA restrictions are harder to challenge than SC ones, so the NC playbook has to be board-level buy-in rather than after-the-fact dispute.

findings.fact: Brunswick County's development ordinance structurally mandates POAs in new subdivisions. Brunswick County UDO Section 6.11.2.H.I requires that all roads not maintained by NCDOT "shall be dedicated to a property owners association," and before final plat approval: the association is responsible for maintenance and upkeep; "The property owners association shall be established before the lots are sold"; "Membership in the association shall be mandatory for each lot buyer and all successive buyers"; and "Any sums levied by the association that remain unpaid shall become a lien on the individual owner's property." A parallel provision requires roads dedicated to a POA or a Road Maintenance Agreement before further subdivision activity. Sunset Beach's UDO likewise assigns operations and maintenance of stormwater facilities to "The POA, HOA Associations, etc., covenants" and contemplates conveyance of infrastructure to an HOA/POA.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is why HOA coverage is so dense in the Brunswick beach towns: county ordinance requires a mandatory-membership POA with lien power for any subdivision with private roads, which describes most of the golf and coastal retirement communities in Sunset Beach, Carolina Shores, Calabash and Ocean Isle. Practical consequence: in unincorporated Brunswick County and the beach towns, assume an ARC approval step on nearly every residential job and sell that as a service. It also means the highest-leverage NC sales channel is the POA board and property manager, not the individual homeowner.

findings.fact: Brunswick County's UDO (revised and readopted March 16, 2015, most recent revision August 19, 2024, PDF footer dated 1/28/2025) defines Impervious Surface as: "Any surface which in whole or in part, restricts or prevents the natural absorption of water into the ground. Such surfaces may include, but not be limited to compacted earth (such as marl and coquina), gravel, concrete, asphalt, or other paving material, and all area covered by the footprint of buildings or structures. Porous pavement, uncovered wooden slatted decks and the water area of a swimming pool are considered pervious." A full-text search of the 491-page UDO returns no occurrence of "artificial turf" or "synthetic turf." The UDO also contains a Water Quality Protection (WQP) Overlay at Section 4.8.7.E requiring development to "Limit the built upon impervious area to no more than 25% of the lot," provide a buffer of at least 30 feet from any wetland or water line, and keep structures at least 75 feet from the mean high water line.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Two takeaways. First, no Brunswick County ordinance regulates artificial turf as such — there is no turf ban, no turf standard, no turf-specific permit; the entire regulatory question is whether it counts as impervious/built-upon, and state law answers that. Second, the 25% WQP Overlay cap is even tighter than the countywide picture, so on WQP-overlay parcels the zero-BUA argument for turf is worth real money. Verify overlay status on the County GIS before quoting.

findings.fact: An independent NC engineering firm (WithersRavenel, article published April 29, 2026) documents the practical effect of the statute for the sports-field market: it cites N.C.G.S. 143-214.7D(b)(6) and states the change "allowed stormwater permitting agencies to treat synthetic fields much like natural grass fields and allowed designers to engineer them with similar stormwater detention systems, creating balance on sites where sports fields needed to be efficiently designed to meet the statutory requirements." The same paper gives NC-specific life-cycle figures for a 100,000 sq ft full-size field: synthetic turf construction $1.75M–$2.25M vs natural grass on amended soil $300K–$400K and sand-based grass with underdrains $1.0M–$1.5M; annual maintenance approximately $15,000–$20,000 for synthetic vs $60,000–$80,000 for natural grass; and cost per hour of use over a 10-year life cycle of $91.69 for synthetic vs $105.07 for basic natural grass and $123.62 for sand-based natural grass, on roughly 2,950 annual use hours for synthetic vs 1,380–1,820 for grass.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The owner wants municipal softball and sports-field work. This is a North Carolina-specific, engineer-authored, citable cost-per-hour case he can put in front of a parks and recreation director or a town council — and the stormwater point is the closer, because a synthetic field in a Brunswick County coastal-county jurisdiction can now be designed without counting as built-upon area. Pair the cost-per-hour table with the 143-214.7D citation in any municipal proposal on the NC side.

findings.fact: There is a genuine technical tension between two North Carolina rules that the installer must resolve in writing. 21 NCAC 28B .0503(b)(1) requires that "the sub-grade is compacted and shall pitch properly to drain," while G.S. 143-214.7D(b)(6) grants the zero-BUA exemption only where the turf is "installed according to the manufacturer's specifications over a pervious surface." Related state rules give a usable benchmark for perviousness: 143-214.7D(b)(3) treats #57 stone at least four inches thick over geotextile fabric as not built-upon area, and both 143-214.7D(b)(4) and the Sunset Beach UDO use a hydraulic conductivity of greater than 0.001 cm/sec (1.41 inches per hour) as the porosity standard.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: A reviewer can reasonably ask how a compacted sub-grade is a "pervious surface." The defensible NC install spec is: compacted sub-grade pitched to drain, then a #57 stone base at least four inches thick over geotextile — which the statute itself already declares not built-upon area — then drainable-backed turf per manufacturer spec. Documenting the assembly that way satisfies the board rule and the statute at once, and gives the PE something to certify at 1.41 in/hr for Sunset Beach. Standardize this assembly for all NC work.

not_found: No ordinance in Brunswick County, Shallotte, Sunset Beach or Carolina Shores that mentions artificial or synthetic turf. Full-text searched: the 491-page Brunswick County UDO PDF, the current Brunswick County Stormwater Ordinance PDF, the Brunswick County Municode Code of Ordinances via the Municode search API, the 488-page Shallotte UDO PDF (amendments through April 2026), the Shallotte Municode code, the Sunset Beach UDO PDF, and the Sunset Beach Municode code. Zero hits for 'artificial turf' or 'synthetic turf' in any of them. The only 'turf' reference in the Sunset Beach UDO is to golf course tee box/fairway/putting green turf. Conclusion: there is no local artificial turf ordinance anywhere in the NC portion of the service area — the question is governed entirely by the state built-upon-area statute and the local impervious-surface definitions.

The Carolina Shores zoning ordinance text itself. Carolina Shores publishes its code through American Legal Publishing (codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/carolinashores/), which is behind a Cloudflare challenge and renders its code content via JavaScript; the town's own website exposes only the Comprehensive Plan (2018), the zoning map (2023) and permit forms, not the ordinance text. I could not read the Carolina Shores impervious surface definition or its lot coverage limits.
