Someone should call the Planning & Zoning Division at 910-575-4877 to confirm whether Carolina Shores' definition of impervious surface has been conformed to G.S. 143-214.7D.

A count or percentage of homes in Brunswick County or its beach towns that sit inside an HOA/POA. No authoritative Brunswick-specific figure exists in any source I could reach. The Foundation for Community Association Research statistical review publishes national figures (373,000 associations, 78.1 million residents) but its public pages do not break out North Carolina or South Carolina. State-level NC figures circulating online (roughly 14,000 associations, 2.75 million residents) appear only on HOA-management vendor blogs, which I would not put in front of a client as a source. What I could source is the structural driver instead: Brunswick County UDO Section 6.11.2.H.I mandates a mandatory-membership POA with lien power for any subdivision with non-NCDOT roads.

Any NC Division of Coastal Management written guidance on whether artificial turf counts toward the 30 percent impervious cap in the Coastal Shorelines AEC under 15A NCAC 07H .0209(d)(2). This matters because G.S. 143-214.7D(b) is worded 'for the purposes of implementing State or local government stormwater programs,' and the 07H AEC cap is a Coastal Resources Commission land-use rule rather than a stormwater program. The DEQ Coastal Management permit pages I could reach do not address it and several DEQ sub-pages 404. This is an open legal question and should be settled by a written determination request to DCM before the client quotes a turf job on an AEC waterfront lot.

The identity of which Brunswick County municipalities hold delegated CAMA local permit officer authority to issue minor development permits (versus which route applicants to the DCM Wilmington regional office). The DEQ Division of Coastal Management minor-permits and local-permit-officer pages returned 404 or unusable content at every URL I tried. Get this from DCM's Wilmington district office directly — it determines who the client calls first on a Sunset Beach, Ocean Isle Beach or Holden Beach waterfront job.

North Carolina versus South Carolina sales and use tax treatment of artificial turf installation (real property contract / capital improvement versus taxable repair, maintenance and installation services). This is a genuine cross-border cost difference for the client's pricing, but I did not research it and will not guess at it. It should be a separate question to a CPA licensed in both states.

applies_to: The full Grand Strand service polygon crossing the state line: Horry County, SC (Loris, Adrian, Allen, Longs, Hand, Wampee, Little River, North Myrtle Beach, Conway, Carolina Forest, Socastee, Myrtle Beach, Surfside Beach, Murrells Inlet, and the "…ddville" town at lower left, almost certainly Reddville/Maddville near the Georgetown line) and Brunswick County, NC (Shallotte, Carolina Shores, Sunset Beach, Ash, Pireway, Longwood, Reeves, Holden Beach). Both counties sit in the Atlantic Coastal Plain flatwoods (MLRA 153A). Findings on soil, water table, heat, storms, pests and litter apply across the whole polygon unless a specific county or city is named.

findings.fact: Horry County's 1986 USDA soil survey maps the county (1,150 sq mi / 736,000 acres) into 10 general soil map units. The largest is Yauhannah-Ogeechee-Bladen at 19% of the county (moderately well to poorly drained), then Woodington-Goldsboro-Pocomoke at 15.5% (poorly to very poorly drained), Nansemond-Pocomoke-Kenansville at 13.5%, and Pocomoke-Echaw-Centenary at 10%. Only two units (Lakeland-Leon-Newhan, 4.5%; parts of unit 2) are dominated by well or excessively drained soils.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The single most useful sales fact in this layer: on roughly two-thirds of Horry County the native soil is a sand or loamy sand that is officially rated poorly to moderately-well drained. That is the opposite of the clay-subgrade problem turf installers face in the Piedmont or the Midwest. On clay you excavate and import stone because the subgrade will not let water through. Here the sand lets water through fine — the constraint is that the water table comes UP into your excavation for part of the year. The base design changes accordingly: you are building for lateral escape and elevation above the seasonal high water table, not for percolation downward. Quote the unit names on a page and a Horry County reader can check them against their own address in Web Soil Survey.

findings.fact: The same Horry County survey states the limitation in plain language: "Wetness and the sandy texture of these soils limit their use as sites for dwellings, local roads and streets, and for most recreation uses," and for the wettest units, "Wetness and ponding severely limit most areas of this map unit for use as sites for dwellings and local roads and streets and for most recreation uses."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the USDA, not a competitor, saying the native ground here is a poor recreation surface. It is the strongest third-party argument for a properly engineered turf base: the reason natural grass fields in Horry County get rutted, muddy and closed in winter is documented in the county soil survey. It also sets the honest counterweight — the same wetness that ruins natural grass will ruin a badly built turf base.

findings.fact: Brunswick County NC's NRCS hydric soils inventory lists the flatwoods series that dominate the county's map units: Leon fine sand (80% Leon, hydric), Murville mucky fine sand (80% Murville, hydric), Torhunta, Rains fine sandy loam, Woodington, plus better-drained ridge units — Baymeade fine sand, Kureb fine sand, Blanton, Norfolk, Onslow, Pactolus, Mandarin, Foreston, Goldsboro, Lynchburg — and coastal Newhan/Corolla/Duckston/Carteret sands and Bohicket tidal marsh.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Same story on the NC side of the line, with a slightly different cast of soil names. It tells you which Brunswick jobs will be easy (Baymeade, Kureb, Norfolk — the sandy ridges under most of the Shallotte/Carolina Shores subdivisions) and which will need real drainage engineering (Leon, Murville, Rains, Torhunta flats). Naming Leon and Murville on a Brunswick County landing page is the kind of specificity a national turf franchise will never write.

findings.fact: NRCS Web Soil Survey rates Leon fine sand "Very limited" for Small Commercial Buildings in Brunswick County, and the stated rating reason is "Depth to saturated zone (1.00)" — 1.00 being the maximum severity value on the NRCS 0.00–1.00 scale. Murville adds "Ponding (1.00)" and "Flooding (1.00)". Baymeade fine sand, 1 to 6 percent slopes, by contrast is rated "Not limited".
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Directly on point for the owner's target market — daycares, pet daycares, commercial pads and municipal fields are exactly what NRCS means by "small commercial buildings." The federal rating for the dominant flatwoods soil is the worst possible score, and the sole reason given is the water table. Any commercial turf proposal on a Leon or Murville site that does not say what it is doing about the saturated zone is a proposal that will fail. This is also the honest answer to "why is your bid higher than the guy from Charlotte?"

findings.fact: Leon series (USDA Official Series Description, poorly and very poorly drained): "The water table is at depths of 6 to 18 inches for 1 to 4 months during most years. In low flats or sloughs it is at a depth of 0 to 6 [inches] for periods of more than 3 weeks during most years. It is between depths of 18 and 36 inches for 2 to 10 months during most years."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: A typical residential turf excavation is 3–4 inches; a pet-turf or sports base is 4–8 inches. On Leon soil in a wet winter you are digging into ground that is already saturated at the depth you are excavating to. That means: no dry sub-base compaction window in Dec–May, imported open-graded stone rather than screenings that will pump, and often raising finished grade rather than cutting. It is also the honest reason a putting green on a Leon flat needs a different detail than one on a Baymeade ridge two miles inland.

findings.fact: Water table depths from USDA Official Series Descriptions for the other dominant local series: Woodington — 0 to 12 inches, December to May, and "A seasonal high water table is within 10 inches of the surface in periods of high rainfall." Ogeechee — +1.0 to 1.0 foot (i.e. up to a foot of standing water above the surface), December to May. Murville — "Depth to the seasonal high water table ranges from 0 to 1 foot from November to May." Rains — 0 to 12 inches, December to April. Goldsboro — 18 to 30 inches, December to April. Yauhannah — within 1.5 to 2.5 feet of the surface "for as much as 4 months during most years," December to March. Baymeade — 45 to 60 inches, December to April.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the technical spine of the whole layer. The range across the polygon is enormous — from standing water above grade (Ogeechee) to a water table four feet down (Baymeade) — and it changes over a few hundred yards. It kills any one-size base spec. Practically: on Baymeade/Kureb/Norfolk ridges a conventional 4-inch compacted aggregate base is fine; on Leon/Woodington/Ogeechee/Murville/Rains flats the base has to be free-draining stone daylighted or tied to a positive outfall, because for four to six months of the year there is nowhere below for water to go. Publishing these numbers with the USDA series names is the single most credible technical thing this business can put on a website.

findings.fact: Saturated hydraulic conductivity of these coastal sands is high in the upper profile: Baymeade 6.0–20 in/hr from 0–36 inches; Woodington 6.0–20 cm/hr in the top 12 inches, dropping to 2.0–6.0 cm/hr from 12–47 inches; Goldsboro 2.0–20 in/hr in the top 15 inches, dropping to 0.6–2.0 in/hr below. Leon is "moderate to moderately rapid in A and E horizons; moderate to moderately slow in Bh horizons" — the Bh (spodic) horizon is the restrictive layer.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Two honest and useful points. First, the surface sand drains beautifully, which is why turf feels like an easy sell here. Second, most of these profiles have a slower layer underneath — Leon's spodic hardpan, Goldsboro's and Woodington's finer subsoil — that perches water. So a percolation test dug 12 inches deep on a summer afternoon will give a flattering number that has nothing to do with February performance. The right test is deeper than the base, and ideally in the wet season.

findings.fact: Penn State's Center for Sports Surface Research measured infilled synthetic turf outdoors at University Park, PA in summer 2011. On 6 June 2011, with air temperature 73–79°F, standard green fibre/black crumb rubber turf read 156.9–169.0°F across the afternoon (average 162.9°F); gold fibre/black rubber peaked at 177.0°F at 1:00 PM with air at 75°F. On 21 July 2011 with air at 88–99°F (hazy and breezy), readings ran 126.6–161.0°F. In the lab, all 11 fibre/infill combinations exceeded 150°F, and the report concludes: "Reductions of five or even ten degrees offer little advantage when temperatures still exceed 150° F."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the honest number the client asked for, from a university lab, not a manufacturer. Note what it actually shows: turf hit 169°F on a 77°F day in Pennsylvania. Air temperature is a weak predictor — solar radiation drives it. It also destroys the "cool turf" marketing claim: Penn State tested cooling fibres, coloured rubber, TPE, EcoFill and AstroFlect and found nothing that mattered. Saying this out loud on the site is the credibility move; every competitor page in Myrtle Beach is claiming their product runs cool.

findings.fact: The New Jersey DEP's 2022 review of synthetic turf, summarising McNitt & Petrunak's Penn State data, states that turf surface temperature "exceeded the air temperature (taken at 3 feet above the ground) by anywhere from approximately 23-32°C (41-59°F) depending on the month the measurements were taken."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This gives a defensible way to convert to Myrtle Beach conditions without inventing a local measurement. It is a state environmental agency, not an industry body, so it survives scrutiny.

findings.fact: NOAA 1991–2020 climate normals for Myrtle Beach (latitude 33.73°N): mean daily maximum 84.5°F in June, 87.4°F in July, 86.5°F in August; record high 104°F (26 June 1952 and 5 August 1954). Applying NJDEP's +41 to +59°F offset to a normal July afternoon of 87.4°F gives an expected turf surface of roughly 128–146°F; on a 95°F day it gives roughly 136–154°F. This arithmetic is derived from the two sourced figures — it is not a Myrtle Beach measurement.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The honest headline for a Myrtle Beach page is something like: "expect 130–150°F on a July afternoon, and a black-infill field can go higher." Presenting it as derived arithmetic rather than a measured local number is itself a trust signal, and it invites the obvious follow-up sale — an infrared thermometer reading taken on the customer's own lawn or field, which costs the business almost nothing and is far more persuasive than any brochure.

findings.fact: A 2018 clinical review in Sports Health (Sage/PMC) reports that "Third-generation infill systems have been reported to have surface temperatures as high as 93°C" — 199°F — and that the surface temperature is driven by total solar radiation because the exposed pile fibres have low specific heat. The same review notes: "A common misconception is that synthetic turf is maintenance free; in fact, however, these surfaces require routine maintenance," including periodic replacement of lost infill to keep infill depth within manufacturer spec, because falling infill depth increases surface hardness and injury risk.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Two things at once. The 199°F figure is the worst-case number a sceptical school board member or parks director will have already read — better to have quoted it first. And the maintenance point is the honest offset that turns into recurring revenue: infill top-up, grooming and depth gauging are a legitimate annual service contract on every municipal field the owner wants to win, and framing them as required (with a peer-reviewed citation) makes the contract easier to sell than framing them as an upsell.

findings.fact: Counterpoint from the peer-reviewed literature, in a climate almost identical to the Grand Strand: Grundstein & Cooper (2020) collected matched Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature data over natural grass, FieldTurf artificial turf and hardcourt tennis at the University of Georgia in Athens, GA every 10 minutes from 9 AM to 6 PM over 24–28 July 2019. Athletic surface type had no statistically significant effect on WBGT in any practice period (midday p = 0.776). At midday, artificial turf ran only 0.83–1.06°C (1.5–1.9°F) higher in dry-bulb temperature than well-watered grass, and its dewpoint was about 1°C lower. Their conclusion: "in a humid, subtropical climate over well-watered grass, there is no difference in WBGT among the three athletic surfaces."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the fact that lets the business handle the heat objection honestly instead of ducking it. The surface is genuinely scorching to touch — that is real and the page should say so. But WBGT, the index every high school athletic association and the NATA actually use to cancel practice, did not differ between turf and grass in a humid subtropical July. The honest framing is: "the surface is much hotter; the heat-stress index at head height, in our climate, measured about the same. Bare skin contact is the real risk, not the air." That reads as a company that knows the literature, and it is far more persuasive than either the industry line or the anti-turf line.

findings.fact: Irrigation does not solve turf heat. Penn State's report cites McNitt et al. (2008): watering "has been shown to rapidly drop surface temperatures immediately after watering; however, temperatures quickly rebound to near pre-irrigation levels." In the underlying work, surfaces at roughly 130–160°F dropped to about 75°F, then rose back to 90–120°F within 30 minutes and stayed there for the rest of a three-hour monitoring period.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Kills the "just hose it down" answer before a customer discovers it themselves. Half an hour of relief is not a management plan for a summer daycare recess. It also argues for design-side mitigation instead — shade structures, morning-use scheduling, and honest siting advice — which is a better conversation than a promise the product cannot keep.

findings.fact: NJDEP's review sets out why children are the highest-risk group on hot synthetic turf: they have "a higher surface area to mass ratio, higher metabolic rate, higher skin temperature, and are less efficient at evaporative cooling"; they are less able to perceive thermal discomfort and so do not self-modify; "due to children's shorter stature, a greater proportion of their body is at closer proximity to the surface"; and they are "at greater risk of experiencing a burn-related injury as they are more likely to be in greater contact with the synthetic turf surface than adults." The memo also documents two known burn incidents on hot turf (a BYU football coach; six Peruvian soccer players with burns and blisters on their feet).
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This lands squarely on the owner's stated target verticals — daycares and pet daycares. It is the objection a daycare director will raise, and it deserves a real answer, not a deflection. The commercially smart play is to own it: recommend shade sails or partial canopy over the play area, specify light-coloured infill even though Penn State says it only buys a few degrees, propose morning-use zoning, and put a surface-temperature check into the maintenance contract. A turf company that arrives at a daycare with a heat-management plan wins against three companies that arrive with a sample and a price.

findings.fact: A 2025 peer-reviewed review in Environments (MDPI) on artificial turf microplastics states that "Combined mechanical stress, ultra-violet radiation, and weathering processes contribute to the breakdown of synthetic grass fibers and infill materials, generating particles ranging from nanometer to millimeter scales," and that these particles "are detected in drainage systems and surrounding soils near sports facilities."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: UV — not salt, not rain — is the documented mechanism that ages the fibre. That reframes the whole coastal-durability conversation correctly: the thing to ask a supplier about is UV stabilisation and warranty terms, and the thing to ask about siting is unshaded southern exposure. It also flags a real environmental exposure on a coast full of tidal creeks and the Intracoastal Waterway — worth pre-empting rather than being caught by it in a municipal procurement debate.

findings.fact: NJDEP, citing the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (2017) and the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department, states it is "best practice not to install synthetic turf fields near or within the 100-year flood zone and areas adjacent to open ocean that are vulnerable to high velocity wave action and storm surge," and further that "in-fill type field not be installed in areas where standing water may frequently occur."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the hardest fact in the layer and the most valuable one to publish. Large parts of the Grand Strand — Murrells Inlet, Socastee, the Waccamaw floodplain around Conway, Little River, the Shallotte River corridor, the Brunswick beach towns — are inside 100-year flood zones. A company that says "we will tell you if your site is wrong for infilled turf" is a company municipal buyers trust with the sites that are right. It also converts: naming the specific places where you would recommend against your own product is the most credible sentence a contractor can write.

findings.fact: On what actually fails in a flood, NJDEP states: "Synthetic turf with pelletized infill, as opposed to carpet-style, is particularly vulnerable to flooding, since the infill material may become negatively buoyant and wash away… If the infill type is selected for installation in areas that commonly experience flooding, preference should be given to infill materials with high specific gravity since these are less likely to wash away." It also notes that "damaged synthetic turf fields are difficult to repair and may require complete replacement."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: A specific, actionable spec decision for this coast: coated-sand or high-specific-gravity infill rather than buoyant crumb rubber on any flood-exposed site. That is a genuine engineering recommendation the owner can put in a bid and defend in a council meeting, and it differentiates from installers who quote one infill for every job.

findings.fact: NJDEP is blunt that a turf field is not pervious cover: "Because these fields are of significant size and their construction necessitates clearing of the land and compacting the soil, they cease to function as pervious cover and thus must be designed to store and slowly diffuse stormwater." It adds that "proper drainage of synthetic grass fields goes beyond the turf's infiltration capacity. The successful installation of a well-draining turf field requires the sub-base material to also drain well," and cites at least one experimental study (Simpson & Francis, 2021) "showing that natural grass outperforms synthetic grass in runoff reduction and water retention."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The honest answer to "turf drains better than grass." Sometimes it does not. On this coast the practical consequence is that a turf field or a large pet-turf yard is a stormwater design problem, not just a landscaping job — which is exactly why commercial and municipal work here needs a contractor who talks to the civil engineer. That is a positioning advantage against residential-only installers, and it is the right frame for the municipal softball field work the owner is chasing.

findings.fact: Local flood magnitude, on the record: during Hurricane Florence (September 2018) the National Weather Service Wilmington office recorded 23.63 inches of rain 2.9 miles WSW of Loris, SC — a South Carolina tropical cyclone rainfall record — and 23.33 inches 7.8 miles SW of Bolivia, NC in Brunswick County. The Waccamaw River at Conway crested at 21.16 feet, "breaking its Hurricane Matthew crest by over three feet." Myrtle Beach airport recorded 9.50 inches.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Loris and Conway are corner points of the client's own service polygon. This is the design event, and it is checkable: 23 inches of rain in one storm. Any drainage claim on the website should be sized against it rather than against a generic "heavy rain." It is also the emotional hook for the flood section — every long-time resident of this polygon remembers Florence and Matthew.

findings.fact: Baseline rainfall for the area, NOAA 1991–2020 normals for Myrtle Beach: 53.56 inches per year, with the wettest months September (6.77 in), July (6.61 in) and August (6.27 in).
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Roughly 4.5 feet of rain a year, concentrated in the hurricane season, over soils that are already saturated for part of the winter. It is the routine load a base has to shed year after year, separate from the once-in-a-decade storm.

findings.fact: North Myrtle Beach adopted a performance-based definition of pervious surface in zoning text amendment ZTX-25-8 (2025). Per the Planning Commission record, "the amendment now defined perviousness based on tested infiltration rates for both the installed surface system and the underlying soil," with permits subject to inspection and the owner responsible for maintaining infiltration performance over time. City staff's ordinance memo for the same amendment sets the threshold at a minimum infiltration rate of two inches per hour.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The two halves of this layer collide here. In North Myrtle Beach, whether an installed turf lawn counts as pervious — and therefore whether it eats into a lot's impervious surface ratio — now depends on a tested rate for the system AND the soil beneath it. On a Leon or Ogeechee flat with the water table at 6 inches in February, passing that test is a design question, not a product question. This is a concrete, local, checkable reason to hire someone who builds the base properly, and it is a page all by itself. (See not_found: the numeric threshold should be confirmed against the adopted code text before publishing the figure.)

findings.fact: Mole crickets, per Clemson HGIC: three species occur in South Carolina — tawny (Neoscapteriscus vicinus, "most destructive to home lawns"), southern and northern. They arrived through "coastal port towns, such as Brunswick, GA, Charleston, SC, and Mobile, AL, during the late 1800s and early 1900s" and spread through southeastern sandy areas; warm, moist soil intensifies activity. The tawny species "feeds almost exclusively on turfgrass roots and shoots"; tunnelling damages putting greens and sports fields; damage peaks "from late August to October." The optimal treatment window is June–July, with a possible second application mid-July to early August, and Clemson states plainly: "A mole cricket management program will not provide 100% control."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Mole crickets are a coastal-sandy-soil pest that specifically wrecks the two things this business sells against — putting greens and sports fields. A natural-grass green in Horry or Brunswick County needs a June–July insecticide programme every year that, by Clemson's own admission, never fully works. Synthetic turf has no roots to eat. That is a clean, sourced, locally specific argument, and it is the strongest pest case for the golf-green product line.

findings.fact: Nematodes, per Clemson HGIC: the sting nematode is "the most destructive nematode" in the region, and "The Sandhills region of the Carolinas and the sandy portions of our coastal areas are commonly infested with the most destructive nematode." Sting nematodes "are generally limited to coarse-textured soils that are high in sand content." Damage is thin, weak turf that cannot take up water or nutrients and is then vulnerable to drought and weeds. On control: "Chemical control in the home lawn is available, but must be done by certified pesticide applicators and can become pricey."
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the pest almost nobody in the sales conversation knows about, and it is essentially specific to exactly this soil type. A homeowner in Carolina Forest or Sunset Beach whose lawn keeps thinning for no visible reason may have sting nematodes in the sand, and there is no homeowner-accessible fix. It is a genuinely useful diagnostic to offer on a blog page ("three reasons your Grand Strand lawn keeps thinning"), and it converts because the alternative — a certified applicator on an annual programme — is expensive and unreliable.

findings.fact: Fire ants, per Texas A&M's fire ant programme fact sheet for turf: red imported fire ants "infest approximately 300 million acres in the United States"; broadcast bait applications made once or twice a year "provide roughly 90% suppression of ants when properly applied"; broadcast treatment is recommended where there are more than 20 mounds per acre. Critically for turf: "Watering turfgrass and bodies of water will attract ant colonies… Conversely, minimizing watering may result in reduced ant nesting activity." Mississippi State Extension adds that "tolerance for fire ants and fire ant mounds is near zero in areas like golf greens, youth soccer fields, cemeteries, or courtyards of elder care facilities!"
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Two honest halves. The favourable half: irrigation attracts fire ants, and synthetic turf is not irrigated — a sourced mechanism, not a marketing claim. The MSU quote is the sales line for daycares, pet daycares and municipal youth fields, where the risk tolerance genuinely is zero. The honest half: 90% suppression is the ceiling even with a proper bait programme on natural grass, and turf reduces but does not eliminate ant pressure — see not_found, because I could not find extension or peer-reviewed evidence either way on ants nesting in installed synthetic turf, and the business should not claim more than it can source.

findings.fact: Live oak (Quercus virginiana), per Clemson HGIC: in its coastal range "Live oak leaves remain on the tree through the winter, then yellow and drop as new leaves expand in the spring." Mature open-grown trees reach "40 to 80 feet tall and 60 to 100 feet wide," with trunks that can exceed six feet in diameter.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: A genuinely local maintenance reality that no national turf page will mention: on the Grand Strand the big leaf drop is in SPRING, not autumn, and it comes with catkins at the same time. A single live oak canopies 60–100 feet — often an entire residential lawn. Turf under a live oak needs blowing in March and April, and the honest sales line is that turf changes the job from raking-plus-mowing-plus-watering to blowing, not that it eliminates work. Saying "your live oak drops in April, not October" in the first paragraph proves local knowledge instantly.

findings.fact: Pines, per Clemson HGIC: loblolly, longleaf and slash pine are the common southern pines for South Carolina. Loblolly needles are 6 to 10 inches long, longleaf 9 inches at maturity and over 12 inches on young plants. On litter: "In the fall, the dropping of interior needles is natural," leaving interior branches yellow or brown while the tips stay green.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Pine straw is the other half of the coastal litter load, and it behaves differently from oak leaves: 6–12 inch needles sit on top of the pile and interlock rather than blowing off, and they shed in autumn. Practically that means a blower and periodic power-brooming, and it means specifying a pile height and infill that release needles rather than trapping them. It also sets up an honest maintenance-package offer for wooded lots in Carolina Forest, Murrells Inlet and the Brunswick County pine flats, which is most of the polygon.

not_found: Salt spray effects on synthetic turf fibres or backing: I found no peer-reviewed or extension-published measurement of what airborne salt or salt spray does to polyethylene turf fibres, latex or polyurethane backing, or seam adhesives over time. The documented degradation mechanism in the literature is UV plus heat plus mechanical wear (Environments 2025 review), not salt. Searches attempted: web search (budget exhausted), Brave/Bing/DuckDuckGo/Mojeek/Ecosia/SearXNG (CAPTCHA or rate-limited), PubMed, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar. Recommendation: do NOT make salt-resistance claims on the site without a source. If the owner wants to address it, the defensible line is that polyethylene is chemically inert to salt and the real coastal question is UV — and that the fasteners are the exposed component (see next item).

Corrosion of turf fasteners and edging in coastal salt air: this is a genuine installation-detail concern (galvanised nails, staples, steel edging, seam nails within a mile or two of the ocean) and almost certainly the right spec answer is stainless or heavy hot-dip galvanised, but I could not source a published corrosion-rate or coastal-exposure standard specific to turf fixings within this session. Worth one targeted follow-up against ISO 9223 atmospheric corrosivity categories or the NC/SC building code coastal fastener provisions before publishing anything.

A published UV-index or UV-dose comparison for Myrtle Beach (33.73°N) versus the northern latitudes where most turf weathering tests and Penn State's heat work were done (State College PA is 40.8°N). The latitude figures themselves are sourced, but I found no published dataset quantifying the difference in annual UV dose, so any statement that turf ages faster here than in the north would be an inference, not a fact. Same for the specific UV-stabilisation test requirement (xenon-arc hours under ISO 4892) in the FIFA Quality Programme or World Rugby Regulation 22 — both handbooks are behind pages I could not retrieve. If the owner wants a UV warranty talking point, get the actual xenon-arc hours and warranty terms in writing from the supplier and publish those.

A published, non-marketing drainage rate (inches per hour) for a specific installed synthetic turf system, and the numeric infiltration threshold in the ADOPTED North Myrtle Beach code. I verified the concept — ZTX-25-8 tests infiltration for both the installed system and the underlying soil — in the Planning Commission packet, and city staff's ordinance memo states a minimum of two inches per hour, but I could not retrieve a stable public URL for the adopted ordinance text to confirm the number. Confirm against Municode or a records request before publishing the figure. Every drainage rate I found for turf products themselves came from manufacturer or installer marketing.

A Myrtle Beach or Horry/Brunswick County pollen count with a published source. There appears to be no AAAAI National Allergy Bureau certified counting station in either county (the AAAAI station directory is JavaScript-driven and I could not enumerate it), and pollen.com's Myrtle Beach page 404s. This is itself potentially useful and honest content — the pollen numbers in weather apps for the Grand Strand are modelled, not measured — but the absence of a station should be verified with AAAAI before it is stated as fact.

Measured surface temperature of artificial turf taken IN Myrtle Beach or anywhere on the Grand Strand. No such measurement exists in any source I could reach. The 128–154°F range in the findings is arithmetic from NOAA normals plus NJDEP's published air-to-surface offset, and should be labelled as derived on any page that uses it. The cheap fix: buy an infrared thermometer, log readings on a few completed installs across a July afternoon, and publish the owner's own data with dates and air temperatures. That would be the only local turf-temperature dataset on the internet and would out-credential every competitor in the market.

Pet paw-pad burn thresholds on hot surfaces. This matters directly for the pet-turf and pet-daycare lines and is widely repeated online (usually as "125°F burns paws in 60 seconds"), but I could not trace it to a veterinary or peer-reviewed source in this session. Do not publish the number without one; the defensible substitute is the sourced surface-temperature data plus a recommendation to check the surface by hand.

Evidence on ants, fire ants or other insects nesting in or under INSTALLED synthetic turf. Everything I found on this was installer blogs and pest-control marketing, split roughly evenly between "turf repels ants" and "sand infill encourages nesting." No extension service or peer-reviewed source either way. The sourced claim the business CAN make is the Texas A&M mechanism — irrigation attracts fire ant colonies, so an unirrigated surface reduces the attractant. Anything stronger than that is unsupported.

findings.fact: HOW TO BID CITY OF MYRTLE BEACH WORK — exact thresholds, from the City's own Procurement Division page. Up to $5,000: purchased directly by designated City employees, no public notice. $5,000.01–$15,000: three quotes obtained by designated City employees, no public notice. $15,000.01–$50,000: three quotes obtained by Procurement staff, posted to online sources. $50,000.01 and over: formal sealed IFB/RFP (RFQ as appropriate), posted online plus legal ad when appropriate. The City posts all solicitations and handles vendor registration through BidNet Direct at www.bidnetdirect.com/cityofmyrtlebeach. Procurement Division: 3231 Mr. Joe White Avenue / P.O. Box 2468, Myrtle Beach SC 29578, (843) 918-2170, procurement@cityofmyrtlebeach.com. Purchasing Division Manager: Ann Sowers, CPPB, NIGP-CPP, CPPO. BidNet vendor support: 800-835-4603 (Option 2). The City operates a LOCAL VENDOR PREFERENCE (LVP): on small-dollar purchases it gives a percentage preference to vendors with a physical location in the City of Myrtle Beach, Horry County, or the NESA (Northeast Strategic Alliance) area; on large-dollar purchases it lets a qualifying local vendor MATCH the low bid. A detailed LVP application is issued with each eligible solicitation and must be completed in full.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the single most actionable item in the whole layer. Three consequences: (1) A single putting green, a small pet-turf pad, or a batting-cage floor under $15,000 can be bought on three phone quotes — no sealed bid, no bonding — so the client's first City job should be deliberately scoped small to establish past performance. (2) A full field is over $50,000 and goes to sealed IFB, which means bid bonds, performance bonds and a formal response. (3) The Local Vendor Preference is a structural advantage over the national turf installers that currently take this work — a Horry County physical address lets him MATCH the low bid on a field-sized job. He must register on BidNet Direct today and complete the LVP application on every eligible solicitation.

findings.fact: SOUTH CAROLINA LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR MUNICIPAL BIDDING. SC Code § 11-35-5320 requires ALL political subdivisions of the State (counties, municipalities, school districts) to adopt their own procurement ordinances embodying 'sound principles of appropriately competitive procurement' — meaning each city and county sets its OWN thresholds, and there is no single statewide municipal bid threshold. For reference, the State's own small-purchase rule (§ 11-35-1550) allows purchases up to $10,000 with no competitive quotes if the price is reasonable; three written quotes for small purchases up to $25,000, or up to $100,000 for commercially available off-the-shelf products, or up to $100,000 for CONSTRUCTION; and advertised small purchases up to $100,000 for non-construction.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Answers 'how does procurement work here' correctly: there is no one SC number. Myrtle Beach's sealed-bid line is $50,000; North Myrtle Beach's and Horry County's are set separately by their own ordinances; the State's construction quote ceiling is $100,000. The practical rule for the client is that he must learn each buyer's threshold individually, and that a job priced just under a given buyer's sealed-bid line is dramatically easier to win.

findings.fact: SOUTH CAROLINA CONTRACTOR LICENSING. SC Code § 40-11-30: no entity or individual may perform or offer to perform contracting work where the total cost of construction exceeds TEN THOUSAND DOLLARS for general contracting without a license from the SC Contractors' Licensing Board. This threshold was raised from $5,000 to $10,000 by 2023 Act No. 69 (H.4115), effective May 19, 2023. The relevant classification for field/site work is General Contractors-Highway subclassification 'Grading', defined in § 40-11-410 as 'the soil preparation and rehabilitation of streets, roads, highways, railroad beds, building sites, parking lots, and storm sewers.' A General Contractors-Building licensee may perform Grading as ANCILLARY work directly associated with a building it was engaged to construct, but that ancillary work cannot exceed twenty percent of total construction cost.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: Hard legal line. Any single SC job over $10,000 — which includes essentially every commercial putting green, every pet-daycare turf pad of consequence, and every sports field — requires a state contractor's license. If the client is not licensed, that alone disqualifies him from every municipal bid in the SC half of the polygon regardless of price. Getting licensed is the first prerequisite, ahead of any bid registration.

findings.fact: NORTH CAROLINA CONTRACTOR LICENSING (the other side of the state line). Per the NC Licensing Board for General Contractors: 'If a project is valued at $40,000 or more, your general contractor must have a license issued by the state' and 'By law, a general contractor must be licensed if the total project cost is valued at $40,000 or higher.'
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: The polygon crosses a state line and the thresholds are FOUR TIMES apart: $10,000 in SC, $40,000 in NC. That means jobs in Shallotte, Calabash, Sunset Beach, Carolina Shores and Ocean Isle Beach between $10,000 and $40,000 can be done with no NC general contractor license, while the same job in Little River or Loris requires an SC license. NC also requires a separate NC license — an SC license does not travel across the line. Two license applications, two sets of paperwork, one polygon.

findings.fact: NORTH MYRTLE BEACH PARK & SPORTS COMPLEX — EXPANSION IS NATURAL GRASS, NOT SYNTHETIC. Construction on the expansion ran May 2024 to November 2025; the first tournament on the expanded fields was February 2026, drawing 70 teams from 14 states. The expansion added five soccer fields, six baseball/softball fields, freshwater ponds, walking trails, two playgrounds and picnic shelters. The complex now totals 12 baseball/softball fields, 13 soccer/lacrosse fields and 16 batting cages at 150 Citizens Circle, Little River SC 29566, with 3 miles of walking trails, five playgrounds, an amphitheater and a nature preserve. The Phase II bid documents (Owner: City of North Myrtle Beach; Architect: Mozingo + Wallace Architects, Myrtle Beach; contract documents dated October 16, 2023; bid date February 27, 2024) put the project value at $40,000,000 on a 93-acre site and specify 'sprigging of playing fields' to achieve 'a full growing season' — i.e. sprigged natural bermudagrass.
findings.why_it_matters_for_turf: This is the correction that protects the client from wasting a sales cycle. The single biggest recent sports-field investment in the polygon — $40 million, 11 new fields — chose NATURAL GRASS, not synthetic. North Myrtle Beach is not a synthetic-turf buyer today. If he pitches them, the pitch is a conversion argument (300+ playing days, tournament rain-outs, sprig grow-in downtime) against a facility that just spent $40M on sod, which is a hard sell for several years. Myrtle Beach (all-synthetic at Styers) is the receptive city; North Myrtle Beach is not.
